messages.subject: Cholesky decomposition:  cholesky_factor_corr
parts:
I have a similar question on estimating the correlation using lkj_corr_cholesky(eta).  For instance,  I have 4*4 correlation  matrix      

    
                            1.0  0.6  0.6  0.6
      Omega_b=    0.6  1.0  0.6  0.1      and  standard deviations, sigma_b=c(0.134,0.182,0.179,0.255) for 4 random effects.
                           0.6  0.6  1.0  0.6
                           0.6  0.1  0.6  1.0


 I am using the relation (b <- mean + (diag_pre_multiply(sigma_b, L_Omega_b)*z)'


where


sigma_b ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
to_vector(z)~normal(0,1);
L_Omega_b ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(2);


Omega_b <-multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega_b);


I am getting the following results:

Omega_b[1,1]      1.000  
Omega_b[1,2]      0.268  
Omega_b[1,3]      0.079  
Omega_b[1,4]     -0.012  
Omega_b[2,1]      0.268  
Omega_b[2,2]      1.000  
Omega_b[2,3]     -0.042  
Omega_b[2,4]     -0.177  
Omega_b[3,1]      0.079  
Omega_b[3,2]     -0.042  
Omega_b[3,3]      1.000  
Omega_b[3,4]     -0.050  
Omega_b[4,1]     -0.012  
Omega_b[4,2]     -0.177  
Omega_b[4,3]     -0.050  
Omega_b[4,4]      1.000  


What is the appropriate value of eta to be used?  I have used 1 and 2 and none of them is estimating the correlations correctly. I am able to estimate the standard deviations well with half Cauchy prior.  Is there something I am doing wrong?


Thanks,


Olive

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cholesky decomposition:  cholesky_factor_corr
parts:
Point means are usually not great estimators — what is the marginal
distribution of each parameter?  This is likely a case where you’re not
constraining the correlations much so that marginal posteriors are
really wide but still consistent with the true values.

95% quantiles?  I would not be surprised if that range
includes the true value of 0.6.

messages.author: 743bbacc59f4b25f
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Cholesky decomposition: cholesky_factor_corr
parts:
On Tuesday, December 1, 2015 at 12:36:17 PM UTC-5, Michael Betancourt wrote:
Right, your posterior captures all of the true correlations!
The problem here isn’t estimation, it’s uncertainty — you 
just don’t have enough data to inform the correlations
all that well.

What Mike says is true, although there is the additional issue that if the true correlation matrix has 0.6 for all the off-diagonal elements and your prior on the (Cholesky factor of the) correlation matrix is much greater than 1, then the prior information you are adding to the model --- that the correlations are probably small --- is not aligned with the data-generating process. In that situation you need even more data to get point estimates of the correlations that are close to 0.6.

Ben
